chapter: Cap, the city and its dances
title: Cap sending for him, the L&N train and eating in New Orleans
summary: Cap and Kid Howard met him at the train station, took him around town and restaurants, and he recalls musicians who slept drunk.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Did you get upset thinking about the brothers over here and your being over there? Did that bother you at all?
No, that didn't bother me over there because one thing, I was Cap's prep. And Cap used to send for me. In other words, he'd send for me.
He weren't completely left out then?

No. Cap used to send for me. And Cap, Kit Howard, George Gano, they'd know what time the L&N train. At that time they had the L&N, you know what I mean? At that time, well, they'd meet the train and they'd come get me from the L&N station. Howard was living on Begunna Street too at that time. And they'd come meet me at the L&N station. And, no, I didn't know anything about the city. Where they'd take me, I didn't know. All I would do was go. I do know one place that Cap told my mother and dad in a letter that he wasn't going to send me back until that Monday night. Well, when I got to the pass, I knew where I was, you know. And Cap brought me to the Humminbird. And where I was located, I can't place it now. So many places he brought me. There's stories of Pelican and this place and that place. And they used to have a place on Howdyville Street, somewhere around the ring, where they had, what was the name? And they had a, Douglas' Restaurant. And they had benches in that restaurant about longest from there to that door there. And, uh, homemade tables. And people used to pay, they packed in, they like that. So we used to go there and eat. When we didn't go to D-Lights, we used to go to E-Lights and eat all the time.
And the menches would be 12 feet long, about. About a 12 foot long men, something like that.

Right. Yeah. And, uh, well, the tables were, you know, they were homemade too. And the table was the same way. You'd be on this side and a big bunch on that side, you know. And, but, things wasn't like it is now. I used to see, when I moved over here, I used to see some of the guys used to, uh, have their instruments. And they would get high on their job, you know. And sometimes you'd see them laying on the side with their horns, with their head on their instruments, you know, laying up their sleep. Like, if somebody, some of the other musicians come along and see them, you know. And they'd take their money out their pocket and take their horns, bring it home. And then when they would wake up, they'd go home, no instrument or no nothing. Ah. And so, but, they would call them up, or you'd go to their house and bring them their money and bring them their instruments. But you better not do anything like that now, you know what I mean? And they used to see you get too high and wouldn't know where you live. All that in there, they didn't sleep. Ain't nobody no body. I mean, there wasn't anyone body.
No, it's true. You can't say that today.
